headline: Automate paycheck splits into sinking funds for fixed expenses, savings, and discretionary spending to remove day-to-day financial admin and mental load
reasoning: Katherine Spitzkowsky advocates for automating personal finances using a 'delegate, eliminate, automate' philosophy so that when a paycheck arrives it is automatically distributed across multiple accounts: one for direct debits and fixed expenses, one for savings, and one for discretionary spending. This structure removes the mental burden of deciding whether a purchase is affordable and ensures savings are built from the first paycheck. She notes clients range from three accounts to as many as 20, with the key being the separation of known fixed costs from variable spending.
quote: your current bank or another bank may give you the option where when your paycheck hits your bank account, you can have it. So that automatically splits out into a number of different savers having sinking funds for fixed expenses. So direct debits for your rent or, you know, subscriptions, that type of thing. And just knowing that that money is to one side, splitting out the stuff for the savings so that we're, you know, building that from day one and then having our spending money and just knowing what's in our transaction account, we can spend. So it takes that day to day admin and mental load away from, oh, can I really afford to buy that? Or, you know, understanding where your money is going to. You know, I have some clients who they're very happy with three bank accounts and I have others who maybe have 15 or you know, up to probably about 20 accounts is probably the most that I've seen.
episode_title: FWIW: What to do with your first paycheck?

headline: Save at least 20% of first paycheck, ensure superannuation is in a cost-efficient fund invested appropriately from day one
reasoning: Katherine Spitzkowsky recommends that young people starting their first job save a minimum of 20% of their paycheck as a foundational rule of thumb. She also emphasises the importance of reviewing superannuation fund selection early, ensuring it is cost-efficient and aligned with the individual's investment preferences. These are presented as the two primary financial priorities upon receiving a first salary.
quote: Obviously, saving is the number one thing that we recommend. And a good rule of thumb to start with is trying to put away at least 20% of your paycheck. So if you could put 20% aside for savings, great. And then maybe you can think about that pair of shoes you have your eye on. And I guess the extension of that is understanding your superannuation. So making sure that it's in the right fund from day one is a big, big tick from all financial advisors out there, making sure it's cost efficient and invested the way that you want it to be.
episode_title: FWIW: What to do with your first paycheck?

headline: Build a three-to-six month emergency fund in a separate high-interest savings account before investing in shares or ETFs
reasoning: Katherine Spitzkowsky advises that before moving into investing in shares or ETFs, individuals should establish an emergency buffer of three to six months of living expenses. This fund should be held in a separate high-interest savings account, ideally one without an associated card, to reduce temptation to spend it and to earn a better rate of return than a standard transaction account. The rationale is to avoid being forced to sell investments at an inopportune time from a tax or market perspective.
quote: So making sure that you've got between three and six months worth of living expenses set aside. So if Bush came to shove, you're not having to sell down shares or investments that, you know, maybe it's not the right time from a tax perspective or from where the market's at. Making sure that your savings are put into a separate account so that there's less temptation for you to be dipping into it. And also, usually our transaction accounts aren't giving us the best rate of return in terms of savings. So putting it in a high interest savings account that we may not have a a card for so that we can't dip into.
episode_title: FWIW: What to do with your first paycheck?
